question: Which statement is true about the SYS_CONTEXT function?

SYS_CONTEXT can only be used inside PL/SQL blocks, never in a plain SQL SELECT statement.
SYS_CONTEXT always returns a NUMBER, regardless of what information is requested.
SYS_CONTEXT requires a table to be specified in a FROM clause other than DUAL.

DELETE ROLE hr_clerk;
REVOKE ROLE hr_clerk;
ALTER ROLE hr_clerk DISABLE;

question:
Which statement is true about a role created WITH the following statement?
CREATE ROLE hr_clerk IDENTIFIED BY secretpwd;

options.text: A user who has been granted this role must supply the password before that role becomes enabled for their session.
IDENTIFIED BY creates a brand-new database user named HR_CLERK with that password.
IDENTIFIED BY has no effect on roles and is silently ignored by Oracle.
The password applies to the DBA who created the role, not to the users it is granted to.

solution: A - A user who has been granted this role must supply the password before that role becomes enabled for their session.

question: A user has been granted several roles. Which statement is true about which of those roles are active by default when the user connects?

options.text: By default, all roles granted to a user are enabled automatically when the user connects, unless the user's default role list has been changed.
No granted role is ever active until the user manually runs SET ROLE for every single one, every time they connect.
Only the DBA role is ever enabled automatically; every other role must always be enabled manually.
A user can have at most one role enabled at any given time.

solution: A - By default, all roles granted to a user are enabled automatically when the user connects, unless the user's default role list has been changed.

question: Which statement is true about granting a role to another role?

options.text: A role can be granted to another role, letting privileges cascade through a hierarchy, but Oracle prevents a role from being granted to itself, directly or through a cycle.
Oracle does not allow a role to ever be granted to another role.
A role can only be granted directly to a named user, never to another role.
Granting a role to another role automatically merges the two roles into a single new role.

solution: A - A role can be granted to another role, letting privileges cascade through a hierarchy, but Oracle prevents a role from being granted to itself, directly or through a cycle.

question: Which statement is true about creating a view with the FORCE keyword, as in CREATE FORCE VIEW emp_v AS SELECT ... FROM a_table_that_does_not_exist_yet?

options.text: Oracle creates the view even though the referenced table does not yet exist, but marks it invalid until a matching table is created and the view is recompiled.
FORCE causes Oracle to automatically create the missing table referenced in the view's query.
FORCE has no real effect; CREATE VIEW always fails immediately if the referenced table does not exist.
FORCE can only be used when replacing a view that already exists, not when creating a new one.

solution: A - Oracle creates the view even though the referenced table does not yet exist, but marks it invalid until a matching table is created and the view is recompiled.

question: Which statement is true about creating an index directly on a view?

options.text: Oracle does not support creating an index directly on a view; indexes can only be created on the actual tables that the view queries.
CREATE INDEX automatically applies to every view based on the indexed table.
An index created on a view is faster than an index created on a table.
A view automatically gets its own index the moment it is created.

solution: A - Oracle does not support creating an index directly on a view; indexes can only be created on the actual tables that the view queries.

question: Which view definition is NOT updatable through simple INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements, because of the DISTINCT keyword?

CREATE VIEW v2 AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees WHERE department_id = 60;
CREATE VIEW v3 AS SELECT * FROM employees;
CREATE VIEW v4 AS SELECT employee_id, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 3000;

question: SCOTT owns the EMPLOYEES table and creates a view, EMP_PUBLIC_V, that exposes only a few non-sensitive columns from it. Which statement is true about granting access to this view?

options.text: SCOTT can grant SELECT on EMP_PUBLIC_V to another user without granting that user any privilege directly on the underlying EMPLOYEES table.
A user must always be granted SELECT on EMPLOYEES directly before they can be granted SELECT on EMP_PUBLIC_V.
Privileges on a view and privileges on its base table are always identical and cannot be granted separately.
Views cannot have privileges granted on them at all; only tables can.

solution: A - SCOTT can grant SELECT on EMP_PUBLIC_V to another user without granting that user any privilege directly on the underlying EMPLOYEES table.

question:

SELECT MAX(AVG(salary))
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;

options.text: A single value: the highest of the per-department average salaries, after the inner AVG is computed for each department and the outer MAX collapses those averages into one result.
An error, because Oracle never allows one aggregate function to be nested inside another.
One row per department, each showing that department's average salary.
The single highest individual SALARY value in the entire table, ignoring departments.

solution: A - A single value: the highest of the per-department average salaries, after the inner AVG is computed for each department and the outer MAX collapses those averages into one result.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id, job_id, SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((department_id), (job_id));
Which statement is true about the result of this query?

options.text: It produces one set of subtotal rows grouped only by DEPARTMENT_ID, and another set of subtotal rows grouped only by JOB_ID, but no combined DEPARTMENT_ID/JOB_ID detail rows and no automatic grand total.
It behaves exactly like GROUP BY department_id, job_id, producing only the detail-level combinations.
It behaves exactly like CUBE(department_id, job_id), producing every possible combination plus a grand total.
It raises an error, because GROUPING SETS requires at least three grouping columns.

solution: A - It produces one set of subtotal rows grouped only by DEPARTMENT_ID, and another set of subtotal rows grouped only by JOB_ID, but no combined DEPARTMENT_ID/JOB_ID detail rows and no automatic grand total.

question: Which statement correctly counts how many distinct job titles exist in each department, for departments that have more than 3 distinct job titles?

options.text: SELECT department_id, COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) > 3;
SELECT department_id, COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) FROM employees WHERE COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) > 3 GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, COUNT(job_id) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING job_id > 3;
SELECT department_id, COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) FROM employees HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) > 3;

solution: A - SELECT department_id, COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT job_id) > 3;

question: Which statement correctly identifies the LAST_NAME values that appear more than once in the EMPLOYEES table?

question: Which statement is true about when the condition in a HAVING clause is evaluated?

options.text: It is evaluated once per group, after the rows in that group have already been aggregated, not once per individual row.
It is evaluated once per individual row, before any grouping takes place.
It is evaluated exactly once for the entire result set, regardless of how many groups exist.
It is evaluated before the FROM clause is processed.

solution: A - It is evaluated once per group, after the rows in that group have already been aggregated, not once per individual row.

question: Which statement is true about a standard B-tree index on a single nullable column?

options.text: Oracle does not create an index entry for a row where the indexed column is NULL, so a query filtering with WHERE indexed_column IS NULL generally cannot use that index.
Oracle stores a special placeholder entry for every NULL value, so IS NULL searches always use the index just as fast as any other condition.
A column that is ever NULL cannot be indexed at all.
An index converts every NULL value in the column to a default value automatically.

solution: A - Oracle does not create an index entry for a row where the indexed column is NULL, so a query filtering with WHERE indexed_column IS NULL generally cannot use that index.

question: Which statement correctly creates an index on EMAIL that also enforces that no two rows can share the same EMAIL value?

options.text: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX emp_email_idx ON employees(email);
CREATE INDEX emp_email_idx ON employees(email) ENFORCE UNIQUE;
CREATE INDEX UNIQUE emp_email_idx ON employees(email);
A regular CREATE INDEX statement always enforces uniqueness automatically, regardless of any keyword.

solution: A - CREATE UNIQUE INDEX emp_email_idx ON employees(email);

question: A sequence was created with CACHE 20, and the instance is shut down abnormally (for example, SHUTDOWN ABORT) before all 20 cached values have been used. What happens to the unused cached values?

options.text: They are lost, creating a gap in the sequence; the next NEXTVAL after the instance restarts continues from a new cached block, not from where the lost values left off.
They are automatically recovered and reused the next time the instance starts.
The sequence is dropped automatically whenever this happens.
Oracle rolls the sequence definition back to its original START WITH value.

solution: A - They are lost, creating a gap in the sequence; the next NEXTVAL after the instance restarts continues from a new cached block, not from where the lost values left off.

question: Which statement is true about a sequence created without specifying MAXVALUE or MINVALUE?

options.text: Oracle applies NOMAXVALUE and NOMINVALUE by default, which set very large effective limits rather than restricting the sequence to a small range.
The sequence cannot generate more than 10 values without MAXVALUE being explicitly set.
Omitting MAXVALUE and MINVALUE causes the CREATE SEQUENCE statement to fail.
Oracle automatically sets MAXVALUE to the same value as START WITH.

solution: A - Oracle applies NOMAXVALUE and NOMINVALUE by default, which set very large effective limits rather than restricting the sequence to a small range.

question: Which statement is true about how aggregate functions such as SUM and AVG handle NULL values in the column they are applied to, by default?

options.text: They ignore NULL values entirely; only COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs, while the other aggregate functions simply skip rows where the relevant column is NULL.
They treat every NULL value as 0 before calculating the result.
They raise an error if the column being aggregated contains any NULL value.
They return NULL for the entire aggregate if even a single row has a NULL value in that column.

solution: A - They ignore NULL values entirely; only COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs, while the other aggregate functions simply skip rows where the relevant column is NULL.

options.text: The sum of the unique SALARY values in department 50, counting each distinct salary amount only once even if several employees share it.
The sum of every SALARY value in department 50, including repeated values from employees who share the same salary.
The number of distinct SALARY values in department 50.
An error, because DISTINCT cannot be combined with SUM.

solution: A - The sum of the unique SALARY values in department 50, counting each distinct salary amount only once even if several employees share it.

question: Which two statements are true about COUNT, when used as COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column_name)? (Choose TWO)

options.text: COUNT(*) counts all rows in the result set, including rows where every column is NULL.
COUNT(column_name) counts only the rows where that specific column is not NULL.
COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name) always return the same result for every table.
COUNT(column_name) counts every row, the same as COUNT(*), regardless of NULLs in that column.
COUNT(*) requires the table to have a primary key defined.

solution: A - COUNT(*) counts all rows in the result set, including rows where every column is NULL. B - COUNT(column_name) counts only the rows where that specific column is not NULL.

It returns every row in the table, regardless of COMMISSION_PCT.

question: Which statement is true about the two arguments passed to the NVL function?

options.text: They should be of compatible data types, because NVL returns a value typed according to the first argument and Oracle must be able to reconcile the two types.
They can always be of completely unrelated data types, such as a NUMBER and a DATE, with no restriction whatsoever.
The second argument must always be a literal value, never a column or expression.
NVL always converts both arguments to VARCHAR2 before comparing them.

solution: A - They should be of compatible data types, because NVL returns a value typed according to the first argument and Oracle must be able to reconcile the two types.

question: Which statement is true about the difference between the RR and YY date format elements when converting a two-digit year with TO_DATE?

options.text: RR can resolve a two-digit year into either the current century or an adjacent one based on its value, while YY always places the two-digit year into the current century, regardless of how far that date is from today.
RR and YY always produce exactly the same date for any two-digit year.
YY can span centuries intelligently, while RR is fixed to the current century only.
RR and YY are only valid for four-digit years, never two-digit years.

solution: A - RR can resolve a two-digit year into either the current century or an adjacent one based on its value, while YY always places the two-digit year into the current century, regardless of how far that date is from today.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id = 10
UNION
SELECT employee_id FROM employees WHERE department_id = 20
ORDER BY employee_id;
Where must the ORDER BY clause appear in a statement that combines two queries with a set operator like UNION?

options.text: Only once, at the very end of the entire combined statement; it cannot be attached to just one of the individual SELECT statements being combined.
It must be repeated identically after each individual SELECT statement.
It can only appear after the first SELECT statement, never after the last one.
ORDER BY cannot be used at all in a statement that includes UNION.

solution: A - Only once, at the very end of the entire combined statement; it cannot be attached to just one of the individual SELECT statements being combined.

question: Which statement is true about the number and data types of the columns used with MINUS, UNION, UNION ALL, and INTERSECT?

options.text: Every SELECT combined by a set operator must return the same number of columns, with data types that correspond position by position across the queries.
Each SELECT in the combined statement can return a different number of columns, as long as the total is the same across all of them combined.
Only the first and last SELECT statements need to match in column count; the others are flexible.
Set operators automatically convert mismatched column counts by padding missing columns with NULL.

solution: A - Every SELECT combined by a set operator must return the same number of columns, with data types that correspond position by position across the queries.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
MERGE INTO employees_bonus b
USING employees e
ON (b.employee_id = e.employee_id)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET b.bonus = e.salary * 0.1
  DELETE WHERE (e.salary < 2000);
What is the effect of the DELETE WHERE clause nested inside WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE?

options.text: After a matched row's BONUS is updated, that row is also deleted from EMPLOYEES_BONUS if the corresponding employee's SALARY is below 2000.
It deletes rows from EMPLOYEES (the source table) instead of EMPLOYEES_BONUS.
It is invalid syntax; MERGE cannot contain a DELETE clause under any circumstances.
It deletes every row in EMPLOYEES_BONUS whenever any single row matches, regardless of the WHERE condition.

solution: A - After a matched row's BONUS is updated, that row is also deleted from EMPLOYEES_BONUS if the corresponding employee's SALARY is below 2000.

question:

It raises an error, because INSERT can only target one table per statement.
It inserts the same row repeatedly into SALES_Q1 until it matches a row already in SALES_SUMMARY.

solution: A - For every row returned by the SELECT, it inserts a corresponding row into both SALES_Q1 and SALES_SUMMARY in a single statement.

ALTER TABLE employees MODIFY salary COMMENT 'Monthly salary in USD';
INSERT COMMENT INTO employees.salary VALUES ('Monthly salary in USD');

question: The DEPARTMENTS table is referenced by a FOREIGN KEY constraint in the EMPLOYEES table. Which statement allows DEPARTMENTS to be dropped along with that dependent foreign key constraint, instead of failing with an error?

question: Which statement is true about the difference between WITH ADMIN OPTION and WITH GRANT OPTION?

options.text: WITH ADMIN OPTION is used when granting a system privilege or a role, while WITH GRANT OPTION is used when granting an object privilege.
WITH ADMIN OPTION and WITH GRANT OPTION are simply two different names for the exact same clause.
WITH GRANT OPTION is used for roles, while WITH ADMIN OPTION is used for object privileges.

solution: A - WITH ADMIN OPTION is used when granting a system privilege or a role, while WITH GRANT OPTION is used when granting an object privilege.

question: Which statement is true about using ORDER BY with a column that is not included in the SELECT list?

options.text: A plain SELECT (without DISTINCT) can ORDER BY a column from one of the queried tables even if that column does not appear in the SELECT list.
ORDER BY can only ever reference a column that also appears in the SELECT list.
Referencing a column not in the SELECT list in ORDER BY always raises a syntax error.

question: Which statement is true about what happens to a pending (uncommitted) transaction when a user exits a SQL session normally, for example by typing EXIT in SQL*Plus?

options.text: Oracle performs an implicit COMMIT of the pending transaction before the session ends.
The pending transaction is always automatically rolled back on a normal exit.
The transaction remains pending indefinitely, even after the session has fully disconnected.
Normal exit has no defined behavior for pending transactions in Oracle.

solution: A - Oracle performs an implicit COMMIT of the pending transaction before the session ends.

question:

It requires an explicit ON clause to specify the join condition, just like an INNER JOIN.

question: Which statement is true about where a NOT NULL constraint can be defined?

options.text: NOT NULL can only be defined as part of the column definition itself (an inline, column-level constraint); it cannot be written as a separate table-level constraint the way PRIMARY KEY or CHECK can.
NOT NULL can only be added as a table-level constraint, never inline with the column definition.
NOT NULL constraints are always automatically generated for every column by Oracle, regardless of how the table is created.
A table can have at most one NOT NULL constraint across all of its columns combined.

solution: A - NOT NULL can only be defined as part of the column definition itself (an inline, column-level constraint); it cannot be written as a separate table-level constraint the way PRIMARY KEY or CHECK can.
